content: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute condition characterized by paralysis due to inflammation of the peripheral nerves. Corticosteroids are hypothesized to provide therapeutic benefits in this condition. A systematic review was conducted to evaluate whether corticosteroids accelerate recovery and reduce long-term complications in GBS. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs comparing corticosteroids or adrenocorticotrophic hormone to placebo or supportive care. The primary outcome was the change in disability grade on a seven-point scale after four weeks. Secondary outcomes included the time to unaided walking, time to discontinuation of mechanical ventilation (for ventilated patients), mortality, combined mortality or disability (defined as inability to walk unaided) at 12 months, relapse rates, and adverse events. The search for relevant studies was conducted on January 12, 2016, using multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, as well as trial registries. No new trials were identified in searches conducted in June 2009, November 2011, or January 2016. Data from six trials involving 587 participants were analyzed for the primary outcome. Moderate-quality evidence indicated that corticosteroids did not significantly improve the disability grade after four weeks compared to control groups. The mean difference (MD) in disability grade improvement was 0.36 less in the corticosteroid group (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.16 more to 0.88 less improvement). In four trials involving 120 participants, very low-quality evidence suggested that oral corticosteroids were associated with less improvement in disability grade after four weeks compared to no corticosteroids (MD 0.82 less improvement; 95% CI: 0.17 to 1.47 grades less). In two trials with 467 participants, moderate-quality evidence showed no significant difference in disability grade improvement after four weeks with intravenous corticosteroids (MD 0.17; 95% CI: -0.06 to 0.39). Moderate-quality evidence also showed no significant difference between corticosteroid-treated and control groups in achieving improvement by one or more disability grades after four weeks (risk ratio [RR] 1.08; 95% CI: 0.93 to 1.24) or in the combined outcome of death or disability at one year (RR 1.51; 95% CI: 0.91 to 2.50). High-quality evidence demonstrated that corticosteroid treatment was associated with a higher incidence of diabetes requiring insulin (RR 2.21; 95% CI: 1.19 to 4.12) and a lower incidence of hypertension (RR 0.15; 95% CI: 0.05 to 0.41). In conclusion, moderate-quality evidence suggests that corticosteroids, when used alone, do not significantly accelerate recovery or improve long-term outcomes in GBS. Very low-quality evidence indicates that oral corticosteroids may delay recovery. High-quality evidence confirms that corticosteroid use increases the risk of diabetes requiring insulin and decreases the risk of hypertension.
